item.title: Challenges for Family Courts and Pathways for Modernization Across Canada
item.description:
Authors: Joanna Radbord, Rachel Birnbaum

Source: Windsor Yearbook of Access to Justice

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution; Canada-related term in title: canada; Canada-related term in abstract: canada

Abstract: We must keep our family justice system aligned with contemporary legal needs and act urgently to address family law reform in accordance with constitutional principles. This article focuses on envisioning the family law rules of court as more complex than reorganizing words on the page and instead considers family law reform as a dynamic process aimed at improving accessibility of programs and services, and ultimately, benefitting the well-being of people. This article presents the results of a qualitative research study. It weaves the narratives of thirty-four family justice participants from across Canada with the literature concerning the family law rules. Seven themes emerge from the interviewees that reflect broad value-based tensions. We must consider more than legal steps and evaluate the social and human impacts on those who are seeking access to family law justice. We conclude...

Source: Unknown source

Abstract: The Indigenous people of Canada are referred to as the First Nation or Aboriginal people of Canada. Their history can be traced as back as AD 100. The Aboriginal people as commonly referred were largely hunters in the early days. There are three categories of indigenous people in Canada: Inuit, Metis, and First Nation. The Inuit primarily inhabit the northern region of Canada, and their hometown is Inuit Nunangat of the Arctic region of Canada. The Metis people are mixed with European and indigenous ancestry and mainly inhabit Canada's Prairie and Ontario regions, with others settling in other parts of Canada. The First Nation people were the original inhabitants of the land that is now Canada, occupying south territories of Arctic Canada. item.description:
Authors: H A J Russell, Andrew Kirkwood, Christine Rivard, M. Cathryn Ryan, Cynthia McClain

Source: Geoscience Canada

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution; Canada-related term in title: canada; Canada-related term in abstract: canada, canadian, canadians, ottawa; Canada-related source title

Abstract: Groundwater provides potable water for approximately a third of all Canadians, sustains two-thirds of the annual baseflow of many Canadian rivers and underpins agricultural, industrial and ecosystem functions in every province and territory. Yet groundwater has received disproportionately little attention in federal freshwater science, monitoring and policy compared to surface water. The low visibility of groundwater as a topic complicates groundwater governance and hinders advancements in resource assessment, scientific understanding and national reporting of data and research, especially given the already complex division of federal, provincial and territorial responsibilities related to water resources. Source: New Phytologist

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Summary Plasmodiophora brassicae , an intracellular biotrophic protist that causes clubroot in crucifers, extensively alters the host endomembrane system for colonization. However, the molecular mechanisms and functions of effectors to achieve this remain poorly understood. Using fluorescent and transmission electron microscopy of P. brassicae ‐infected Arabidopsis, we show that host endomembranes and organelles become closely associated with P. brassicae secondary plasmodial structures and are subsequently phagocytosed by the pathogen. PbALE is a secreted endomembrane‐targeting effector that binds a range of phospholipids. Overexpression of the effector results in plants with glossy leaves that progressively become chlorotic. Source: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)

Abstract: Generative models of protein structures have accelerated scientific discovery. However, the leading structure-prediction models are trained primarily on crystal structures, limiting their ability to sample the conformations of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can probe the diversity of IDP conformational ensembles, but these simulations are slow and costly. Authors: Doug Doucette

Source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Abstract: This paper turns the structural theory of gap-protected oscillations into measurable monitoring procedures. It distinguishes three levels of conclusion: certified by rigorous bounds, statistically certified with confidence, and estimated from fits without error control. item.title: Variance and local log-concavity of Poisson–binomial laws
item.description:
Authors: Brett Reynolds

Source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Let W be the number of successes in independent trials with unequal success probabilities, with probability mass function f and variance V ≥ 1, and let D be the first index at which f decreases. The normalized Turán deficit δ_k = 1 − f_{k−1}f_{k+1}/f_k², a measure of local log-concavity, is a bounded transform of the discrete curvature of log f at k; for a normal density of variance V, that curvature is 1/V. Quantitative log-concavity is used to derive concentration and log-Sobolev inequalities for discrete laws, but for Bernoulli sums the known lower bounds on δ_k depend on the number of summands or on the success probabilities. We prove V·δ_D ≥ 1/4, and binomial laws show that no constant above 1/3 is possible. With cubic inequalities of Hillion and Johnson, this gives δ_k ≥ 1/(4V + |k − D|) on the whole support. Ultra-log-concavity alone gives no variance-scaled lower bound on δ_D....

Abstract: The dimethyldihydropyrene photochromic system is a 14π-electronic framework that switches to a less-aromatic, nonplanar system under visible light. In this work, we unravel a neutral phosphorus heteroatom-appended dimethyldihydropyrene (DHP) photoswitchable system that acts as a self-sensitizer, enabling precise, wavelength-selective control over singlet oxygen capture with dual reactivity. The attachment of the phosphorus directly to the DHP scaffold allowed red light (640 nm) to selectively generate a phosphinate intermediate (DHP-2), while green light (525 nm) triggers further transformation into an endoperoxide. Abstract: The paper asks how protected oscillations in gap-protected Hamiltonian systems fail. It distinguishes three levels: loss of a certificate, loss of the structural protection itself, and actual dynamical failure. Each stronger level implies the weaker one, but not conversely. Two failure kinds matter: escape from a neighbourhood, and exchange of action between modes. Linear instability cannot occur along a continuous family without the second-order resonance gap first tending to zero; systems with definite energy cannot exit linearly while they remain definite.
